item.title: My unsupported Kindle runs Linux now, and it's more useful than when it was new
item.itunes:title: My unsupported Kindle runs Linux now, and it's more useful than when it was new
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
My 2015 Kindle Paperwhite is officially out of support, and Amazon won't be sending it another update. On paper, that makes it e-waste with a nice screen. But that ignores something important about every E Ink Kindle Amazon has ever sold.

It runs Linux. It always has.

Once I jailbroke it and logged in as root, that old Paperwhite turned into a tiny ARM computer with a touchscreen, a front light, and Wi-Fi. It now runs a current build of KOReader, an Alpine Linux chroot, and has spent time on my wall as a touchscreen Home Assistant display.

I stopped using cloud weather APIs after setting up a local environmental station, and my HVAC automations run flawlessly

My automations shouldn't rely on someone else's data.

By  Jasmine Mannan

Amazon stopped updating my Kindle, but the Linux underneath never left

A frozen firmware is the best thing that can happen to a jailbreak

The Kindle Paperwhite 3 launched in June 2015, and Amazon has supported it for a long time by gadget standards. Since 2021, Amazon has promised at least four years of security updates after a Kindle was last sold on its own store. That's fair for an e-reader, but the clock always runs out.

For my Paperwhite, it ran out in 2023. When firmware 5.16.3 arrived that August, older Kindles stopped getting updates, and mine is frozen on 5.16.2.1.1. The Linux kernel underneath was built on August 1, 2023, which makes it one of the last things Amazon ever compiled for this device.

Here's the thing: on a current Kindle, jailbreaking is a race against Amazon's over-the-air updates, and every new firmware can close the hole you used. Even the newest browser-based jailbreak, Véra, only works up to a specific firmware version on supported models.

My Paperwhite will never get another update. Whatever jailbreak works today will still work in five years, and nobody at Amazon will patch it shut. An unsupported Kindle is a frustrating e-reader to own, but it's the perfect one to tinker with.

I used lightweight Linux to revive a Windows PC that Microsoft gave up on, and it's not Ubuntu

An aging 2012 laptop shed its bloat and booted in minutes with a stripped Fluxbox setup that sips under 500MB of RAM.

4
By  Abhishek Kumar Mishra

Root access shows you exactly how Amazon built it

Jailbreaking doesn't replace the OS, it hands you the keys

There's a common misconception that you have to "flash Linux" onto a Kindle. You don't, and on most models you can't. postmarketOS can replace the whole OS on a Kindle 4, but it leaves you with a worse e-reader. A jailbreak takes a much simpler route: it gives you root on the Linux system Amazon already ships.

My Paperwhite already had KUAL (the Kindle's homebrew launcher) and USBNetwork, which turns the USB cable into a network link. Getting SSH working still took me longer than I'd like to admit. My keys live in 1Password, not in a file, so SSH had nothing to offer and kept asking for a root password. Once I saved the public key where SSH expected it, I had a root prompt over USB.

The first thing I ran was an inventory. It's a fascinating snapshot of a 2015 gadget:

Component

What the Kindle reports

Firmware

5.16.2.1.1

Kernel

Linux 3.0.35-lab126, built August 1, 2023

SoC

Freescale i.MX 6SoloLite on a board Amazon calls "Wario"

CPU

One ARM Cortex-A9 core at roughly 1GHz, with NEON

RAM

502MB, no swap, 213MB available with the stock UI idle

System partition

437MB, 92% full

User storage

3.0GB usable

That's a kernel line from 2011, which Amazon kept patching and rebuilding right up to the end. The biggest single user of memory is Amazon's reader app, KPPMainApp, which holds 66MB of RAM even when nothing is open. Sure, a single core and half a gigabyte isn't much, but it's plenty for a box that only needs to draw text on an E Ink screen.

Microsoft called Linux a cancer, and now it ships a real Linux kernel inside Windows

Microsoft loves Linux now, it seems.

4
By  Adam Conway

The Linux tools that actually work on a 2015 Kindle

eips, LIPC, and a KOReader that still gets updates

With root, Amazon's device becomes yours. The Kindle talks to its hardware through an internal message bus called LIPC, and you can poke it straight from the shell. One command reads the battery level, and another sets the front light anywhere from 0 to 24, so I flashed mine to full and back off from my desk just because I could.

The tool that sold me is eips, which draws text directly on the E Ink panel. Type this over SSH, and your words land straight on the screen:

eips 5 20 "Hello from SSH - this Kindle runs Linux"

Then there's KOReader, which is the reason most people jailbreak in the first place. It handles EPUBs, PDFs, and comics far better than Amazon's reader, and it updates itself over Wi-Fi. Mine jumped from a December 2025 nightly to v2026.07.2, a stable build from this summer, in a few minutes. Amazon gave up on this hardware in 2023, and the open-source community is still shipping it current software. The update did leave an 84.2MB package behind, though, which is a hefty chunk of the few GB that my Kindle has for total storage.

Newer Kindles have the storage to run Alpine properly

The most ambitious thing you can run is a full Alpine Linux chroot, and the alpine_kindle project lists the Paperwhite 3 as its only tested device. It uses a 2GB disk image, which took my free space from 2.4GB down to about 425MB. It works, too. It mounted and dropped me into a shell, with 237MB of RAM to play with and Python 3.7.4 and Chromium already installed.

But that image is an Alpine development snapshot from August 2019. Alpine has rotated its package-signing keys since then, so every repository returns an UNTRUSTED signature error, and you can't install anything new. I also tried the launcher's own updater, hoping it would fetch something newer. It warned me it would use 98% of my free space, deleted my working image, rebuilt it over nine minutes, left me with 39.6MB free, and delivered the exact same 2019 build.

That's where newer Kindles win. Models with 16GB or more of storage can fit the same 2GB image without sacrificing your library, and current jailbreaks like Véra cover the Paperwhite 5 and 6 (both Colorsoft models) and the 2022 and 2024 Scribes. Storage makes Alpine practical, though, not fast.

I turned my Kindle into 4 things Amazon never intended, and now it's the most useful device on my desk

A jailbreak opened it up for several practical uses.

1
By  Samir Makwana

A forgotten Kindle makes a brilliant touchscreen Home Assistant panel

Although I had to port it from the Paperwhite 2 to the Paperwhite 3's sharper screen

Home Assistant made my Paperwhite more useful than when it was new. I run a fork of 1RandomDev's kindle-smarthome-dashboard, which turns a Kindle into a live, tap-to-toggle Home Assistant panel. Most Kindle dashboards just display a screenshot of your Home Assistant dashboard on a timer. This one keeps a live connection, so tapping a button actually switches a light, and changes in Home Assistant show up on the E Ink screen without waiting for a refresh timer.

The upstream project only supports Paperwhite 2, and its layout assumes that model's 1024x758 screen. The Paperwhite 3 panel is 1072x1448, so I pinned the layout to 1448x1072 in landscape and scaled the spacing and fonts up by roughly 1.41x. I also switched brightness control to the LIPC front-light command, because the raw backlight path differs between Kindle models.

Running isn't the same as working

The dashboard needs a small Node.js proxy that translates the Kindle's ancient WebSocket support into something modern Home Assistant understands. I moved it into an LXC on Proxmox on the same host as my Home Assistant VM, and systemd happily reported it as running for four days. It wasn't working at all.

Node 20 on Debian 13 needs a flag to enable its built-in WebSocket client; Home Assistant had moved to a new IP address; its access token was no longer valid; and the Kindle's token didn't match the proxy's. That last one was the sneakiest, because the proxy silently refused the Kindle and left ten dead connections hanging. Lesson learned: check the logs, not the status light.

The other catch is power. That live connection keeps the Kindle from ever going to sleep, so the battery drains quickly, negating one of the benefits of E Ink. The upstream project suggests a small hardware mod that feeds USB power straight to the battery terminals, but keeping it on a charger works too.

Here's what makes Home Assistant work so well in my smart home (and it's not the army of Zigbee sensors)

Making it as beginner-friendly as possible.

2
By  Rich Edmonds

Is it worth jailbreaking an old Kindle?

An unsupported Kindle has nothing left to lose, and frozen firmware means your jailbreak will keep working forever. Mine went from an abandoned e-reader to an SSH-accessible Linux box that reads books better than it did new and doubles as a smart home panel.

Just go in with realistic expectations. You get a 2023 kernel, a 2019 Alpine image, and a single 1GHz core, so this is a tinkering platform, not a tablet replacement. Check your firmware version under Settings -> Device Options -> Device Info before you start. If your old Kindle is gathering dust, there's a surprisingly capable Linux computer hiding inside it.

Yes

item.title: I set up Claude Code the way Spotify does to save tokens, and it cost me more
item.itunes:title: I set up Claude Code the way Spotify does to save tokens, and it cost me more
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
One thing I'm always aware of when handling agentic tasks is my token burn. Simple tasks like generating test files from a template or skimming through a folder of PDF documents to answer a question are almost insulting to the power of a frontier model. That's less of a concern with subscription pricing, but with API billing, token costs add up. Unnecessarily, when a cheaper model (or even a local one) could handle the task.

One of Spotify's engineers fixed this issue by creating two new AiKA Modes in Portal, the managed developer platform the company built internally and later released as a product. Now, I don't have access to that platform, but what I do have is Claude Code and access to a variety of other LLMs. I rebuilt the two modes in my own setup to see what it did to my token burn, but it didn't go exactly as I expected.

I built a website with Claude Code and Stitch 2.0, and now I understand why developers are switching

Although I also understand why every website looks the same now

2
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Spotify's shunt plugin hands Claude Code's grunt work to a cheaper model

Getting it running broke a few things

Shunt's pitch is simple: most of what a coding agent does isn't thinking; it's reading. When Claude Code tries to read a file over 350 lines, a hook blocks it and points Claude at a bulk-reader skill, which sends the files to a cheaper worker model and returns a short summary. A second skill, code-writer, does the same for boilerplate like test files, writing the result straight to disk, so Claude never generates it.

Spotify's numbers are impressive. Against a 162,000-line Java monorepo, the shunt README reports 82% to 94% savings on large reads, with a mean of 90%, using Gemini 2.5 Flash as the worker. The catch is that the worker lives behind Spotify Portal, the company's commercial developer platform, and getting access means talking to sales.

Luckily, the plugin is open source, and the Portal dependency lives in exactly one file. I replaced it with a version that sends the same requests to Lemonade Server running Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B or to Claude Haiku through a headless Claude Code session. Haiku is the closest match to Spotify's setup, and the local model is the one you can run for free.​​​​​​​

Three things broke before I measured a single token, and each is worth knowing. First, shunt's hooks don't work on the current Claude Code. They tell Claude Code to "allow" a command, a value the hook format no longer accepts, so every allowed command threw an error until I made them return nothing instead.

Second, my local model was quietly reading garbage. On Lemonade's ROCm backend, Qwen3-Coder invented function names that don't exist, and when I asked it to copy the first five lines of a file, it returned an opening code fence and stopped. item.title: A Fire TV Cube costs $200 now, and my 2019 Nvidia Shield TV still does more
item.itunes:title: A Fire TV Cube costs $200 now, and my 2019 Nvidia Shield TV still does more
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Amazon recently bumped the price of the Fire TV Cube to $200. That change came quietly in August: the device, which once retailed for $140, suddenly saw a $60 price increase while still offering the same basic hardware. I was particularly shocked by this increase, although I shouldn't say it was that unexpected because RAMageddon has been affecting every industry that uses memory technology.

Still, I was surprised to see a $200 price tag on a device that is worse than the one I purchased about seven years ago. I'm talking about my Nvidia Shield TV, which is now almost seven years old. Compared with the Fire TV Cube, which is now $200, the Nvidia Shield TV still does more.

Nvidia Shield TV still smokes the Fire TV Cube any day

It's not even close

Credit: Amazon

On paper, the Fire TV Cube looks more modern. It supports newer codecs such as AV1 and VP9 Profile 2, comes with Wi-Fi 6E, and includes HDMI 2.1 input and output. But once you move beyond basic streaming and start looking at what these devices can actually do, my seven-year-old Nvidia Shield TV still pulls ahead.

The biggest advantage is lossless audio passthrough. The Shield TV can pass through Dolby TrueHD, Dolby Atmos, DTS:X, and DTS-HD Master Audio directly to a receiver, making it the better device for a proper home theater setup. The Fire TV Cube still struggles with true lossless passthrough for several high-end Blu-ray audio formats, which is difficult to excuse now that it costs $200.

The Shield TV Pro can also function as a full Plex Media Server, thanks to its 64-bit architecture. That means I can connect storage, host my media library, and stream it to other devices without needing a separate computer or NAS. The Fire TV Cube uses a more restrictive 32-bit architecture, so it can't fill the same role. It may be a capable Plex client, but the Shield TV can run the entire show.

Also, I wouldn't say the Shield TV is faster than the Fire TV Cube, because the latter has an octa-core processor that makes navigation smoother. However, when you compare the two devices side by side, the difference isn't exactly huge. Given that my seven-year-old Shield TV can open Netflix, boot up, and scroll through apps and settings almost as quickly as the Fire TV Cube, which is supposed to feature the latest and greatest hardware, it's difficult to justify that $200 price tag.

To be fair, the Shield TV is beginning to show its age. It's limited to Wi-Fi 5 and HDMI 2.0, while the Cube offers Wi-Fi 6E and HDMI 2.1. The Tegra X1+ also lacks hardware decoding for newer formats such as AV1 and VP9 Profile 2.

Amazon's refreshed Fire TV Stick 4K is faster, but the switch to Vega OS comes with a major catch

Say goodbye to Android app sideloading.

1
By  Patrick O'Rourke

Nvidia Shield TV even supports cloud gaming

Amazon Luna can never match the experience

The Nvidia Shield TV's gaming capabilities are another reason why this seven-year-old streaming box is still more capable than the Fire TV Cube. Nvidia's graphics background is baked into the Shield TV's DNA, and GeForce NOW effectively turns the device into a cloud-powered gaming console. I can stream demanding PC games from Steam, the Epic Games Store, and Xbox Game Pass at up to 4K resolution and 60 FPS without keeping an expensive gaming PC in my living room.

Getting started is also fairly straightforward. I can pair almost any Bluetooth controller, including an Xbox or PlayStation controller, launch GeForce NOW, and begin playing. With a fast, stable internet connection, latency is low enough that many games feel surprisingly close to running locally. That is quite an achievement for a streaming device released in 2019.

Amazon technically has an answer in Luna, but the experience on the Fire TV Cube is not nearly as complete. Luna is primarily limited to 1080p at 60 FPS, so it cannot match the sharper 4K streaming available through GeForce NOW on the Shield TV. Its smaller, rotating catalog and publisher-specific channels also feel more restrictive than a service that lets me stream hundreds of supported PC games I already own.

The Nvidia Shield TV is still the undisputed king of streaming boxes

Truly unprecedented hardware

  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 

The Fire TV Cube is not the only device that struggles to beat the Nvidia Shield TV. You can put almost any streaming box next to it, regardless of whether it comes from Amazon, Google, Xiaomi, or another manufacturer, and the Shield TV still holds its own. In many cases, it will do far more than devices released years after it.

That is because Nvidia did not build the Shield TV like an ordinary streaming box. It was massively overpowered when it launched, and that extra headroom is what has kept it relevant for so long. While other companies have spent years releasing cheaper devices with slightly faster processors or marginally better wireless connectivity, few have tried to match the Shield TV's combination of raw performance, physical connectivity, and software freedom.

Just look at the ports. The Shield TV Pro gives me two USB 3.0 ports and proper Gigabit Ethernet, which means I can attach large external drives, transfer files at sensible speeds, and run a complete Plex Media Server directly from the box. Most modern streaming devices give you a single power connector and expect everything else to happen through the cloud. The Shield TV lets me build an entire local media setup around it.

I replaced my Fire TV Stick with a mini PC, and now my TV does things Amazon never intended

Upgrading to a high-quality streaming experience.

item.title: I replaced ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Perplexity with free open-source alternatives
item.itunes:title: I replaced ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Perplexity with free open-source alternatives
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
While my bank already hated to see Apple Music, Spotify, Canva, Adobe Creative Cloud, iCloud+, Google One, Netflix, and about half a dozen other subscriptions coming every month, I know AI tools have made an already existing problem significantly worse. Now, practically every AI tool I use wants its own cut too. Claude Max, ChatGPT Plus, Google AI Pro, Perplexity Pro, Cursor Pro, and so on.

Unlike the subscriptions I listed at the very beginning, though, AI subscriptions overlap a lot more. Spotify and Canva are solving completely different problems. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Perplexity, and Cursor, on the other hand, can all do many of the same things —they just tend to be better at different parts of the job.

That overlap is exactly what made me wonder how many of them I actually needed to be paying for. Instead of looking for one open-source app that could somehow replace everything, I decided to rebuild the different parts of my AI workflow with free, open-source alternatives and see how much I could get away with.

Jan

My local LLM finally feels (well, looks) like ChatGPT

After analyzing the kind of tasks I use AI for, I've realized local LLMs can handle the bulk of my work quite easily. Sure, there are inevitably tasks where I still want the stronger reasoning, larger context windows, or specialized tools that come with frontier models, but most of what I ask AI to do on a normal day really isn't that demanding.

While I initially relied on Ollama and LM Studio for all my local AI needs, Jan ended up being a much better fit for what I was actually trying to replace. Ollama primarily positions itself as a way to run and build with open models, while LM Studio focuses on making local AI easy to run on your computer. Jan's pitch is a lot more aligned with what users like me want. It's described outright as an open-source replacement for ChatGPT and Claude.

After using it, I can see why. The biggest difference is that Jan doesn't feel like I'm opening an app just to run a local model. It feels like I'm opening an AI assistant. The interface is very ChatGPT-like. I can keep separate conversations and Projects, create custom Assistants with their own instructions, upload files, switch between different models, and connect extra tools through MCP.

Getting a model running is also much less intimidating than the phrase "local LLM" makes it sound. Jan has its own model hub connected to Hugging Face, so instead of downloading GGUF files manually and figuring out whether your laptop can actually run them, you can browse models from inside the app. It's also not local-only, and ships with about a dozen of remote providers. This means I can use Jan for both my local and cloud models.

What really sold me on it, though, is that going local doesn't automatically mean giving up all the extras I've gotten used to with ChatGPT. Jan has web search and page fetching built in, so supported models can still pull in current information instead of being stuck with whatever they were trained on. And if I want to take things further, MCP lets me add things like browser control and other external tools!

Though Ollama is excellent at running models, I've found that Jan is much better at handling everything around them. It feels like a middle ground between Ollama, LM Studio, and Open WebUI!

Vane

Perplexity, minus the Pro plan

Vane, previously known as Perplexica, has long been advertised as an open-source alternative to Perplexity, and I can see why! At its core, Vane is an AI-powered search engine that searches the web, pulls together relevant information, and gives you a summarized answer with sources attached. So, basically, the reason I use Perplexity in the first place.

The difference is that Vane can run with local models through Ollama, which means I don't necessarily need to send every question off to another company's servers. It uses SearXNG underneath for web search, and I can choose between different search modes depending on what I'm doing. Speed Mode is there when I just want a quick answer, Balanced Mode is meant for normal searches, and Quality Mode digs deeper when I actually care about the research. I can also narrow searches down to things like the general web, discussions, or academic papers instead of throwing every source type into the same pile.

That sounds fairly basic on paper, but it's exactly the kind of stuff that makes Perplexity useful to me. I rarely open it because I want to have a long conversation with an AI. I open it because I want to ask a question, get something reasonably current back, and immediately see where the information came from.

Vane supports image and video search, lets me upload files and ask questions about them, can restrict searches to specific domains, and even has widgets for things like weather, calculations, and stock prices! That said, Vane is nowhere near as frictionless as just opening Perplexity.com and using it. You need to go through the hassle of setting it up, and Docker is the recommended route. However, once it's running, I get most of the parts of Perplexity I actually care about without paying for another AI subscription.

Open Design

My second designer doesn’t need a subscription

While a Claude subscription was once limited to the actual Chat panel, it’s since expanded into much more of a full-fledged workspace. You get Claude Code, Cowork, and a relatively newer feature called Claude Design. One of the best use cases I’ve personally found for AI is using it as a secondary designer.

I’m not a very creative person, and I spend way more time than I can afford perfecting slide decks, posters, infographics, and even content for socials. That’s why I’ve been experimenting a lot with Claude Design since it launched. It can take a prompt and turn it into things like slides, one-pagers, prototypes, and other polished visual assets. You can then edit them right within the interface using prompts or by tweaking individual elements yourself. This makes it feel a lot less like a one-and-done image generator and more like having a second designer sitting beside you.

However, once I tested Open Design, a completely open-source alternative built around the same idea, I never really felt the need to keep paying $20 just for access to something like Claude Design. Open Design is local-first and lets you use the AI agent you already prefer as the actual design engine.

That can be Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, or several others, rather than locking you into Anthropic’s models. It can generate things like websites, prototypes, slides, images, and other visual assets, and the output stays as actual files you can keep working with instead of living inside a closed platform.

That flexibility is probably what I like most about it. I can keep the same general prompt-to-design workflow I liked in Claude Design, but I’m not tied to a single model or subscription to do it. If I want to use OpenCode one day and Gemini CLI the next, I can. I can also bring in my own design system through a DESIGN.md file, so the output can follow the same colors, typography, spacing, and overall style instead of starting from scratch every single time.

Open Code

Claude Code and Codex, but I get to pick the model

For the longest time, the only reason I could justify my Claude subscription was Claude Code. I've developed a fairly good system around it at this point, and I use it for everything from fixing tiny bugs to making changes across entire projects. While it's excellent at what it does, the catch is, yet again, that I'm bound to Anthropic's models only. Codex has been my current favorite, but it comes with the exact same problem: I can only use OpenAI's models with it.

Given that different models have different capabilities, I feel like locking an entire coding workflow to one provider is unnecessarily limiting. There are times when Claude is better at understanding a messy codebase, times when an OpenAI model handles a task better, and plenty of smaller jobs where I really don't need to be paying for a frontier model at all.

That's exactly where OpenCode comes in. It gives me most of the things I've already built my Claude Code workflow around, including a dedicated planning mode, Skills, MCP server support, and the ability to actually read and make changes across a project. The key difference is that the agent itself isn't tied to one company's models. I can swap between Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, or even local models depending on what I'm working on, without having to rebuild the rest of my setup around them.

Open Notebook

NotebookLM, but I call the shots

As an added bonus, this entire experiment also made me realize there was another AI subscription I probably didn't need to keep around. I've written about NotebookLM far more than any normal person reasonably should, and I still think it's one of the best AI tools Google has made. However, a huge part of why I use it comes down to the features it built around my sources rather than the chatbot itself.

Open Notebook gets surprisingly close to replicating that. I can upload my own sources, ask questions grounded in them, generate summaries and notes, and even create NotebookLM-style Audio Overviews from the material I've added. That's easily one of my favorite NotebookLM features, since I can turn a pile of notes, readings, or research into something I can listen to instead of sitting down and going through everything again.

Of course, NotebookLM still has more polish and some newer features Open Notebook doesn't completely replicate. But if the main things I want are source-grounded chat, summaries, notes, and Audio Overview-style podcasts, Open Notebook covers a surprisingly large chunk of why I use NotebookLM in the first place.

I’m not a very creative person, and I spend way more time than I can afford perfecting slide decks, posters, infographics, and even content for socials. That’s why I’ve been experimenting a lot with Claude Design since it launched. It can take a prompt and turn it into things like slides, one-pagers, prototypes, and other polished visual assets. You can then edit them right within the interface using prompts or by tweaking individual elements yourself. This makes it feel a lot less like a one-and-done image generator and more like having a second designer sitting beside you.

However, once I tested Open Design, a completely open-source alternative built around the same idea, I never really felt the need to keep paying $20 just for access to something like Claude Design. Open Design is local-first and lets you use the AI agent you already prefer as the actual design engine.

That can be Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, or several others, rather than locking you into Anthropic’s models. It can generate things like websites, prototypes, slides, images, and other visual assets, and the output stays as actual files you can keep working with instead of living inside a closed platform.

That flexibility is probably what I like most about it. I can keep the same general prompt-to-design workflow I liked in Claude Design, but I’m not tied to a single model or subscription to do it. Open Code

Claude Code and Codex, but I get to pick the model

For the longest time, the only reason I could justify my Claude subscription was Claude Code. I've developed a fairly good system around it at this point, and I use it for everything from fixing tiny bugs to making changes across entire projects. While it's excellent at what it does, the catch is, yet again, that I'm bound to Anthropic's models only. Codex has been my current favorite, but it comes with the exact same problem: I can only use OpenAI's models with it.

Given that different models have different capabilities, I feel like locking an entire coding workflow to one provider is unnecessarily limiting. There are times when Claude is better at understanding a messy codebase, times when an OpenAI model handles a task better, and plenty of smaller jobs where I really don't need to be paying for a frontier model at all.

That's exactly where OpenCode comes in. It gives me most of the things I've already built my Claude Code workflow around, including a dedicated planning mode, Skills, MCP server support, and the ability to actually read and make changes across a project. The key difference is that the agent itself isn't tied to one company's models. I can swap between Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, or even local models depending on what I'm working on, without having to rebuild the rest of my setup around them.

Open Notebook

NotebookLM, but I call the shots

As an added bonus, this entire experiment also made me realize there was another AI subscription I probably didn't need to keep around. I've written about NotebookLM far more than any normal person reasonably should, and I still think it's one of the best AI tools Google has made. However, a huge part of why I use it comes down to the features it built around my sources rather than the chatbot itself.

Open Notebook gets surprisingly close to replicating that. I can upload my own sources, ask questions grounded in them, generate summaries and notes, and even create NotebookLM-style Audio Overviews from the material I've added. That's easily one of my favorite NotebookLM features, since I can turn a pile of notes, readings, or research into something I can listen to instead of sitting down and going through everything again.

Of course, NotebookLM still has more polish and some newer features Open Notebook doesn't completely replicate. But if the main things I want are source-grounded chat, summaries, notes, and Audio Overview-style podcasts, Open Notebook covers a surprisingly large chunk of why I use NotebookLM in the first place.

item.title: I paid for gigabit internet and discovered almost nothing in my house can actually use it
item.itunes:title: I paid for gigabit internet and discovered almost nothing in my house can actually use it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When you sign up for a new 1Gbps fiber or cable internet package, you might not stop to look at your household ecosystem: smart home bulbs, streaming boxes, tablets, IoT gadgets, and background servers. Realistically, none of them really need, utilize, or physically process a gigabit of bandwidth during normal operation.

You might run a speed test on your phone or main PC, watch the gauge max out at 940 Mbps, and feel a brief wave oftechnological satisfaction. However, gigabit internet has become a security blanket between Wi-Fi physics constraints, server-side throttling, and everyday workload limits. Paying for gigabit speed is largely a marketing-driven exercise in number chasing for most modern households.

Here's why your Plex server feels slow even on Ethernet, and a $10 fix is the answer

Your TV has an Ethernet port, but it's woefully underequipped for a media server

17
By  Tanveer Singh

Will your devices at home use a gigabit?

The answer is probably no

Most everyday devices can't actually reach gigabit speeds because architectural constraints prevent them from saturating a 1G pipe.

The first issue is the Wi-Fi physical layer. Even with modern Wi-Fi 6, 6E, and 7 clients, devices sitting in the same room as an access point, real-world wireless overhead, contention, and distance drop throughput down significantly. You might be getting closer to roughly 400 to 700 Mbps over the 1 Gbps that you're paying for.

This doesn't even consider when you're moving away from it. Go over to the next room from your router, and the signal drops even further through the drywall or a floor, and your speeds dip even more.

You might also deal with a lot of server-side bottlenecks. Your ISP might deliver a pristine gigabit stream to your ONT box, but downloading a file from a game server like Steam or Epic, an update repo, or a video stream like Netflix 4K will max out at 25 to 40Mbps. This means that you're essentially at the mercy of these providers' bandwidth limits and content delivery network throttling.

Audit your household to decide whether gigabit internet is worth it

Sometimes it might be

Before investing in gigabit internet, do a household workload audit. Examine what your devices are actually doing versus what gigabit marketing promises. Many of your smart home and IoT devices won't use gigabit internet at all. If you've got dozens of smart bulbs, smart plugs, and temperature sensors running on 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi or Zigbee, they consume mere kilobytes per second and don't need blistering speeds.

Move on to more general consumption and a look at media streaming. Streaming multiple simultaneous uncompressed 4K Blu-ray rips or high-bitrate Plex streams internally across your local NAS requires local network switching capacity rather than external internet bandwidth. And as addressed earlier, if you're using external streaming platforms, you'll face server-side bottlenecks anyway.

And lastly, it's worth considering the single-user fallacy. A single human can realistically only actively consume or generate data for one high-bandwidth task at a time. More general internet use, like browsing Reddit, writing code, or attending a Zoom call, requires a fraction of a gigabit, so it won't be anywhere near as demanding as a gigabit plan.

There are some instances where gigabit actually does matter. Some niche workloads aren't a marketing gimmick, and you might actually use it. For those who are into heavy, frequent torrenting and game drops, if you're a power user downloading 100 GB AAA game titles daily or syncing massive terabyte-scale media libraries off-site to Backblaze B2, a gigabit upload/download link can save a significant amount of waiting time.

And if you've got a multi-user heavy household (like a large family or a shared home lab where multiple users are simultaneously downloading massive files, hosting remote game servers, or running intensive cloud workflows), a gigabit connection might be worthwhile.

There are other ways to optimize your network

From Ethernet down to access points

Realistically, for the majority of users, even power users, gigabit internet is not fundamental because so many devices in your home can't take advantage of it. You're better off downshifting or optimizing your current network rather than paying extra to upgrade.

The most important element of your network is hardwiring where it counts. Whether you pay for gigabit or not, you shouldn't ever expect Wi-Fi to prove its worth. You should run Cat6 Ethernet drops to your desktop, home server, and main TV streaming box to capture that wire-speed throughput.

There are a range of other ways that you can optimize the actual Wi-Fi in your home too. It can be as simple as repositioning your router to make sure you're taking advantage of RF physics. Or it might be worth investing in another access point or mesh Wi-Fi system so Wi-Fi can reach dead zones in your home much more effectively.

Review your ISP tiers and see whether dropping to a 300 or 500Mbps plan can save you money while making no noticeable difference in daily web browsing, remote work, or streaming performance.

Gigabit internet provides very little value

The majority of users won't see the benefit

Gigabit internet is an incredible engineering feat, but for 90% of connected devices in a modern home, it provides very little value. It's essentially like driving a Ferrari in a school zone. There are many other ways to optimize your home network, whether that's running Ethernet to key devices or repositioning your router. Audit the devices in your home and decide whether you're paying for real utility or just buying peace of mind through a bigger number on your ISP bill.

item.title: Your M.2 slot does more than SSDs, but nobody talks about the boring cards that prove it
item.itunes:title: Your M.2 slot does more than SSDs, but nobody talks about the boring cards that prove it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
For most people, the M.2 slot on the motherboard is synonymous with NVMe SSDs. After all, that is the most common thing people install in their M.2 slots. However, it wasn't made for SSDs exclusively; it was meant to accommodate high-speed as well as low-speed devices. The latter is where non-SSD expansion cards come into the picture.

When you want to add an expansion card to your motherboard without blocking a PCIe slot, the M.2 connector is the best option. It uses the same PCIe bus, offers enough room, and doesn't limit performance, unlike USB adapters. M.2 expansion cards can seem boring, but they can be the most impactful upgrades you can make to your PC. You just need to buy one with a matching key, depending on your motherboard.

I used my spare M.2 slot for something boring, and it became my favorite PC upgrade

An unused M.2 slot can add more than just another SSD.

2
By  Abid Ahsan Shanto

microSD card adapter

microSD card slots are a rare breed

Credit: Wikimedia Commons

microSD cards used to be huge only a few years ago when expandable storage on smartphones was a thing. Even today, if you're a creative professional and your work requires a microSD card slot, it's hard to find one on most laptops, let alone desktops. However, you can convert a spare M.2 slot on your laptop or desktop into a microSD card slot with a simple adapter.

Bringing back this lost functionality to your work device, whether it's a laptop or desktop, is inexpensive. Both A+E and B+M key variants of M.2-to-microSD adapters are available for under $20.

M.2 to microSD card adapter
See at Amazon
I ditched 2TB SSD upgrade plan for a 1TB microSD card, and the speed difference matters way less than I expected

Not all my files need expensive NVMe storage.

9
By  Abid Ahsan Shanto

Capture card

Yes, M.2 capture cards exist

Most capture cards exist in the PCIe form factor, and for good reason. High-performance capture cards need enough PCIe bandwidth and heat dissipation for optimum performance. That said, if you're looking for a capture card without using a PCIe slot, some manufacturers offer M.2 variants, too. These cards are mostly intended for SFF PCs and utilize the PCIe 2.0x4 configuration.

Streaming your gameplay without hurting gaming performance requires a dedicated capture card on many PCs. An M.2 capture card uses the PCIe bus without using a physical PCIe slot, making it better than a slower USB capture card. These can be too expensive for the majority of users, but can make sense for the right user in the right system.

Magewell Eco Capture AIO M.2 capture card
$325 at B&H
Why I'm only making two gaming hardware purchases in 2026

I'm ditching upgrades and going for new experiences.

7
By  Samarveer Singh

SATA adapter

You can never have enough SATA ports

For data hoarders and power users who keep running out of SATA slots, an M.2-to-SATA adapter is a godsend. It allows you to add extra slots for additional hard drives and SATA SSDs. You don't need to replace your motherboard simply because you have a huge game collection, ever-growing media collection, 4K RAW files, or home lab deployments.

Hard drives are obsolete for many use cases, but they're still great for secondary and archival storage. Users who don't want to buy a NAS can get a $20 adapter to install more HDDs on their one-stop rig.

M.2 to SATA 3.0 Adapter Card
See at Amazon
I wish this secret SATA trick had been more popular

SATA is on the way out as a primary storage interface, and it's a shame this trick wasn't used more

1
By  Ty Sherback

Ethernet and Wi-Fi cards

Networking is serious business

If you want to add Wi-Fi to an old PC using an M.2 slot, you can do so with a M.2 Wi-Fi adapter for under $25. These cards use E or A+E key M.2 slots, so inspect your motherboard before getting one. If your motherboard only has an M-keyed slot, you can get an M-to-E-key adapter and plug the Wi-Fi card into it.

Users who have an older Ethernet port can upgrade to, say, a faster 2.5 GbE port using an M.2 Ethernet card. These network expansion cards usually come in the PCIe variety, but as always, you can get an M.2 variant, depending on your system variables and preferences. These adapters also use the A+E key slot on the motherboard.

Nicgiga AX210 BT5.3 M.2 Card
See at Amazon
M.2 A+E key 2.5Gb Ethernet Network Card
See at Amazon
I stopped paying extra for motherboards with Wi-Fi built in, and a $30 PCIe card does it better

Discrete Wi-Fi adapters can step up your PC's networking game

5
By  Tanveer Singh

M.2 expansion cards aren't always exciting, but they do the job

Not everyone would want to install an expansion card into their spare M.2 slots, but they can be extremely useful on the right system. Whether you want to add missing features on old PCs without using your PCIe slots or upgrade existing functionality without spending much, M.2 cards are worth exploring.

item.title: After a month switching between Claude Code and its open-source rival, I only open Claude for one kind of task
item.itunes:title: After a month switching between Claude Code and its open-source rival, I only open Claude for one kind of task
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Most people reach for Claude Code first, and for good reason, since it's the dominant agent. The catch is the usage limits. Every paid plan draws from a single pool shared by Claude chat, Claude Code, and Claude Design, so going hard in one of them chips away at the others. Once that pool's empty, you either sit tight until the reset or pay standard API rates on top of what you're already paying for the subscription.

This is why many are flocking to cheaper alternatives, one of them being OpenCode. It's an open-source coding agent that isn't tied to any one AI company, so you can plug in whatever model you like, including a handful of free ones. After a month of bouncing between them, things did eventually sort themselves into a pattern for my workflow.

Want to stay in the loop with the latest in AI? The XDA AI Insider newsletter drops weekly with deep dives, tool recommendations, and hands-on coverage you won't find anywhere else on the site. Subscribe by modifying your newsletter preferences!

What OpenCode is actually good for

It's built for trying things without counting prompts

I first tried OpenCode out of curiosity. Then it turned into my fallback for whenever I didn't feel like burning through my Claude usage. These days it has a real spot in my stack, and it handles a lot more than I expected, mostly thanks to the way it deals with models.

The model picker is wild, with 75+ providers to choose from, and since every provider you connect sits in one list, you can swap mid-session. Big Pickle and the other free models are fine for chores, and a paid model only becomes necessary when the job actually calls for one. So for the small stuff, like having a script explained or checking a small component, it can all be handled for free, and spending a paid prompt on that stuff almost feels like a waste now.

The fact that it's a terminal tool was my original hang-up, but I've been made aware that there is a desktop app now, which is still in beta. It also reads Claude-style skills from the same .claude/skills folders (with some caveats, which I'll get into) so anything you've built for Claude Code doesn't have to completely stay stuck there.

I tested Claude Code against 3 open-source alternatives, and one came surprisingly close

Claude might not be the only coding agent worth using.

8
By  Anurag Singh

The one job Claude Code still gets

Everything else can be an experiment, this can't

The one task that sends me back to Claude Code is anything on the systems I actually live in. My Obsidian vault is the big one, along with the /index/ project manager I built inside it, but my vibe-coded projects and the artifacts I use every day end up in the same pile. Those don't get to be experiments since I actually use them every day. They have to work the first time because if something goes wrong I'm the one dealing with the fallout.

The /index/ skill is a good example. OpenCode can load it, technically, but the free models I tried would follow it a bit loosely and drift away from the format I'd set up. Part of that is the skill file itself. Claude Code lets a skill carry extra settings at the top, like making it run only when I type /index or limiting which tools it can touch, and OpenCode only reads a handful of basic fields and ignores the rest. Those settings are what keep /index/ from wandering around my vault, so in OpenCode it's running without them.

Then there's undo, which was a pretty big oversight on my part when I first thought I could just bring over my whole workflow into OpenCode. OpenCode has undo, and it rolls back file changes, but only for files inside a Git repository (a version-history system you add to a folder). My vault isn't one, so OpenCode's undo doesn't cover it. Claude Code's checkpoints don't need Git - it saves a file's state before each edit and I can rewind from there, although changes made through bash commands aren't tracked, so it's not 100% bulletproof.

So it's not one single feature that pulls me back into Claude. It's these small things that add up: the models, skills, and undo. And I'd rather hand off my existing tasks to a system I've already built them in and trust.

I switched from Claude Code to Codex for a week, and the trade-offs surprised me

One week, two tools, a lot of opinions.

29
By  Mahnoor Faisal

What each one actually costs me

Neither side is free, including the free one

Claude is ultimately a subscription, and I pay for it because of the entire ecosystem - Claude Design, the artifacts, projects, the Claude Code GUI with the built-in browser, and the workspace features. Large and long projects here tend to push me into usage credits, which are billed at the standard API rate on top of the subscription. And again, since the limits are shared across the Claude surfaces, a heavy day in one of them eats into the rest. This is honestly the biggest limiting factor of Claude, and I don't really have much else to complain about.

OpenCode is free but it still costs me, just in a different way. The free models are capable but thinner than Claude's, there's no question about it. They're great for planning and experimentation, but I probably wouldn't let one loose on my vault. Anthropic also blocked Claude subscription logins in third-party tools earlier this year, and OpenCode pulled its Claude login after a legal request, so to keep using Claude Design and artifacts, I have to keep the subscription regardless of where I can access Claude models.

I use OpenCode over Claude Code, and it's every bit as good

Beat-for-beat, feature-for-feature.

9
By  Mahnoor Faisal

Free covers a lot, just not everything

OpenCode turned into the place where I can give things a spin, and only a few weeks in I noticed that I stopped handing stuff to Claude that I wouldn't be upset to lose. I think if OpenCode's undo ever works without Git, I might consider a switch, though the free models would need to stop drifting from my /index/ skill first, and that feels further off.

item.title: I squeezed my entire network stack onto a Raspberry Pi Zero, and it broke my assumptions about what's essential
item.itunes:title: I squeezed my entire network stack onto a Raspberry Pi Zero, and it broke my assumptions about what's essential
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Self-hosting starts with basic items and can evolve into a complex setup with the best possible hardware. The progression becomes necessary for a better overall experience and system responsiveness. Some projects can benefit from a cheaper yet functional alternative. When you think of a home network stack, you might think of an old laptop, network switches, or even enterprise servers. I won't deny that these components can deliver better performance.

However, I was curious about experimenting with an SBC for a basic networking stack. I put everything I needed on a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, and the setup didn't disappoint. It serves as a network-wide DNS resolver and ad blocker, along with a few other monitoring tools.

Getting the correct tools and SBC OS

DietPi is a perfect pick

It's been hard to convince me to switch to another Raspberry Pi operating system ever since I installed DietPi. I'm amazed by its expansive set of tools, huge set of preconfigured software packages, and resource-frugal nature. DietPi can run on barely 70MB of memory, the lowest in my tests. I compared it with Armbian and the official Raspberry Pi OS Lite, and both needed more than 100MB to run.

A quick flash with the official Raspberry Pi Imager tool prepped the SD card for DietPi. I usually prefer pre-configuring the wireless network and other settings to directly access the SBC via SSH. But this time, I added a USB-to-Ethernet adapter to the Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W. It's more stable and is better if you want to use the SBC for networking projects.

I squeezed DietPi onto a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, and it replaced my $50-a-month cloud setup

DietPi’s lean footprint unlocks a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W that hosts secure backups, ad filtering and browser tools.

By  Abhishek Kumar Mishra

After that, I decided to create a quick network stack of Pi-hole and Unbound. The former would block DNS requests, while the latter would act as a recursive DNS resolver. With this combination, I wouldn't need to rely on Google or other DNS providers. Apart from that, Tailscale was a worthy addition to the setup as it enabled remote access and HTTPS support. The tools in my stack don't need HTTPS support, but it's great to have an option. I installed Tailscale directly via a curl command before moving on to the Docker setup.

All tools live as Docker containers

Only Tailscale exists outside

Docker and Docker Compose were painless to install because of DietPi's software utility. After setting up Docker, I deployed Pi-hole and Unbound as containers. Dealing with all the networking configuration to make Unbound connect and handle DNS requests from Pi-hole was a pain. Once set up, I had these two containers running with the Pi-hole web portal active.

I also had to modify the router's DHCP settings and set the Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W’s IP address as the DNS server. The router sends the DNS requests to the SBC, and the container listens on port 53. Most users simply deploy Pi-hole and let it handle DNS filtering and resolving. But I use Unbound as a resolver, which helps me avoid public providers like Google.

I use these 5 tools to turn my Raspberry Pi into a self-hosting behemoth

Even a Raspberry Pi can become a containerization war machine with the right set of apps

By  Ayush Pande

Usually, you'll find such a setup on a laptop or a dedicated machine. But I was surprised to see it work so well for my home devices. It's a bliss to avoid ads and trackers on most pages, and if you use an ad-blocking extension, the overall experience is much better. Pi-hole can't block ads in apps like YouTube, but that's a small price to pay. I'm happy that most websites now load without bothersome advertisements.

One thing to note is that I don't have that many devices requesting DNS queries in my home. Only my Windows PC and phone need a DNS resolver. Other phones usually cycle between apps and rarely used browsers. So the Pi server has less load. If you have a lot of users and multiple devices, performance might differ.

Monitoring the server

Beszel and Glance handle everything

While I can access the Pi-hole dashboard via the web portal, having a separate monitoring tool is better. Prometheus and Grafana are the common choices, but I use Beszel. My SBC doesn't have the computing power to run heavy monitoring tools, and Beszel doesn't need much. It can track system resource consumption and has a nice graphical interface to view everything. I can even configure it to trigger alerts when CPU or another component usage reaches a certain limit.

Lastly, adding a dashboard makes all the setup nice and tidy. I don't need to frequently open an SSH window to check Docker containers or open the Pi-hole dashboard. Glance is a lightweight tool just like Beszel, and I have a simple DNS dashboard setup inside it. On the left, it shows the status of all Docker containers running on the system. If a container is down, I can immediately notice it and SSH to the SBC.

Setting up a local DNS was one of the easiest improvements I made to my home network

Having local control opens up so many possibilities

14
By  Joe Rice-Jones

​​​​​

On the right side, I have two big panels. Glance embeds the Beszel web interface in an iframe, pulls data from the agent, and displays it. I can see CPU, memory, and display usage with uptime details. Below it is a Pi-hole widget, which is available via the Glance community widgets catalog. It shows the main graphs for queries, blocked items, and domains that the current list covers. It's not an interactive dashboard, but I'll modify the Docker container presentation to redirect to their actual web URLs.

Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W continues to surprise me

Most projects, like a media server or local cloud storage, suffer on this SBC. But my network stack works without problems, with no noticeable lag, and stays responsive. I've used it for some time and never encountered any page load issues except when the internet connection was down. All the DNS requests are now offloaded to the SBC and not to a public DNS provider. The setup barely uses 50 percent of memory and only 10 percent of disk storage. So I can add a few more lightweight containers if needed.

Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W

The Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W is a small SBC with Wi-Fi and Bluetooth connectivity.

item.title: I ditched Google TV's cluttered home screen for a lightweight launcher, and the setup took less time than brewing coffee
item.itunes:title: I ditched Google TV's cluttered home screen for a lightweight launcher, and the setup took less time than brewing coffee
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
There's a lot to love about Google TV — it supports a wide variety of apps, it has some nifty features, and it performs relatively well on affordable devices. However, the platform also has drawbacks, especially with its home screen.

I got tired of Google TV's cluttered recommendations for TV shows and YouTube videos, and the way the UI buries essential settings and access to the Google Play Store. So I've been trying out launchers to replace my home screen — and FLauncher provides one of the most user-friendly options out there.

What is FLauncher?

A lightweight launcher for Android TVs

FLauncher is an open-source launcher for Android TV and Google TV devices. It even works on Chromecasts. It's free and ad-free, making it a great alternative for people who see ads on their Google TV home screen. The app lets you choose which apps appear on your home screen, which wallpaper you use, and lets you customize categories and reorder the apps within them.

Unlike full Android launchers, Google TV launchers don't replace your entire UI; they only replace your home screen. This means that you can still enjoy all the native features that come with your device, as well as features like Google Photos screensavers. FLauncher essentially gives you a more streamlined start page.

FLauncher is effortlessly simple to set up

My new home screen was ready to go in minutes

When I installed FLauncher, I was surprised by how quickly I had it up and running. As soon as I launched the app, I already had a streamlined home page ready to go. This default page included all of my TV apps. I didn't get lost in settings or customization options either—it was extremely easy to access the launcher's configuration options. These settings focus mostly on your Applications, Categories, and Wallpaper. You can also use this menu to access your Android TV settings.

The Applications menu lets you see your installed apps at a glance. I find this tab particularly helpful because Google's default home page tends to bury some of your installed apps. It always feels like I'm setting out on a journey when I just want to head to the Google Play Store. The tab also allows you to uninstall any apps you no longer use. This menu includes a view that allows you to see all the apps you've hidden from the home screen.

The Categories menu lets you create different categories and assign various apps to them. This can be useful if you use your TV device for more than just streaming. Or maybe you have multiple family members who want to prioritize different apps. Since I live alone, I kept the default TV Applications category and slimmed it down to my most-used apps. I long-pressed on an app icon on the home page to bring up a menu that lets me hide these apps.

The Wallpaper menu does what it says on the tin — it lets you select a wallpaper. Unfortunately for me, the Unsplash options didn't work, and I didn't want to load a file manually. So I just used one of the gradient options included in the app. This is an area where I'd like to see more variety and dark mode options.

Overall, though, setting up the new launcher took less than five minutes, including my customization.

It does have a noticeable drawback

No built in home button remapping

Since FLauncher is still in early development, according to its GitHub page, it lacks a major feature: the ability to remap your remote's home button. To do this, you need to use an app called Button Mapper. I mostly avoid button-remapping tools because they can add extra lag to Google TV performance.

Another way to remap your Home button is to disable the default launcher on your Google TV, but this requires ADB commands and can cause issues with your device. I went with Button Mapper as this was the simplest method. Setting up the app was easy, and it let me bind FLauncher to my Home and Apps buttons. This made it easy to access the launcher from my remote.

This didn't add significant time to the setup process, either. Since Button Mapper is also simple to use, it just took another two minutes to remap the buttons on my remote. However, I hope FLauncher builds this functionality in the future.

4 useful Android TV apps that do more than stream movies and TV shows

Android TV apps you didn’t know you needed

4
By  Parth Shah

You can have a new Google TV home screen in just a few minutes

While FLauncher isn't packed with features, it's perfect for minimalists. It's one of the quickest ways to get a new home screen up and running on your Google TV device.

A bonus is that it doesn't interfere with other Google TV features, so you don't have to say goodbye to your Google Photos screensavers. If you want a launcher that's a bit more feature-rich, you should check out Projectivity Launcher. However, I'm also keen to see where FLauncher goes next.

FLauncher

item.title: I turned my old Windows Home Server into a dumb NAS for Plex and Jellyfin
item.itunes:title: I turned my old Windows Home Server into a dumb NAS for Plex and Jellyfin
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
15 years ago, I ran Windows Home Server on an HP MicroServer for reasons I can't fathom now. As I've done more with self-hosted media, my library has kept growing, along with my storage needs. Storage isn't cheap, and neither is a new NAS. I stumbled across that old server and thought, there's probably still some life in it if I repurpose it as a dumb NAS for a few files.

I needed to fill a storage gap, at least temporarily, and thought this could work with the right software and the extra hard drives I had lying around. I cleaned it up and used an open-source project meant to restore legacy servers like this one.

A legacy server

With a bloated operating system installed

The server I was running Windows Home Server (WHS) on is an HP ProLiant MicroServer N40L. It has modest hardware by today's standards: an AMD 1.5 GHz dual-core Turion II processor, 8GB DDR RAM, and four 3.5-inch SATA drive bays. You can also install a fifth drive in the optical-drive bay by removing the top.

I blew the dust out of the server, connected a keyboard and mouse, and an old monitor since it only has a VGA adapter. I powered it on to make sure it worked and to remember the files I had on it a decade and a half ago. I also wanted to know where the storage was at. I expect legacy software to be slow on old hardware, but it was painfully slow just to look up a few drive details. The server's hardware was spry in its day. But WHS was never responsive — I don't know why I enjoyed using it back then.

I knew erasing any data on the old server wouldn't be a problem. I just wanted to make sure it powered on and know which drive WHS was installed on. When I first found it, only two drives were in the bay, with a third halfway pulled out. So, I wasn't sure if it would turn on, let alone let me make it a dumb NAS.

5 open source OS options for your self-built NAS

Break free from the constraints of prebuilt NAS devices.

6
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Creating a dumb NAS

An open-source minimalist OS to the rescue

To restore the server and make it work the way I wanted, I knew it needed to be light and easy on system resources. I chose OpenMediaVault (OMV), an open-source, Debian-based Linux OS that was perfect for the job. Despite the server's age, OMV lets me use it for file sharing, which is all I need. It doesn't bog the system down with a heavy OS.

It's easy to install on the server from a bootable USB drive created using Rufus. I installed the OS first, then found three 1TB drives lying around to use as storage. Once installed, I switched to managing the server through its web-based interface. I did a "quick format" of each drive as ext4 so they were readable and had room to store the files I was about to load on them.

The OMV web interface is straightforward and intuitive, making it easy to manage and monitor the health of the installed drives. Occasionally, the web UI fails to load. Or, I may have a network connectivity issue and need to connect my old monitor to the server to run ovm-firstaid from the prompt, but it's rare.

OpenMediaVault

Openmediavault is a next-gen NAS operating system built on Debian.

See at Official Site

Media server reborn

A new device for self-hosted media

Once the drives were formatted and ready to use, I added shared folders and granted the required permissions. I connected to the legacy machine, created a new folder, and transferred a couple of TV show files to test it. When that worked, I started ripping movies and shows directly to the folders I'd created on the drives. I also started some housekeeping by moving some content from existing folders to my new dumb NAS.

I added new content to my Jellyfin and Plex servers, which was as straightforward as ever. Everything from the dumb NAS plays as smoothly as before, as long as I keep devices hardwired into the network. UHD content buffers over Wi-Fi, which it tends to do in other spots of my setup, anyway. I don't plan to keep this as a permanent media solution, but it can serve as temporary storage. For now, I can watch modern UHD movies from a legacy backend.

10 of the best plug-ins for your OpenMediaVault NAS

Turn your OMV NAS into a behemoth of a storage server with these incredible plug-ins

By  Ayush Pande

Giving an old server a new purpose and solving a need

When I glanced at the old machine and realized I still had the server, I didn't know if I could salvage it. But all I needed was some extra network storage. It might seem like overkill for only 3TB of media storage, and I wish I had larger drives, but I made the best of what I had.

Overall, I'm glad I did this project since it at least gives me temporary storage. It gave me the chance to get to know OMV, and the dumb NAS will get me by until I can invest in a more permanent storage solution.

Creating a dumb NAS

An open-source minimalist OS to the rescue

To restore the server and make it work the way I wanted, I knew it needed to be light and easy on system resources. I chose OpenMediaVault (OMV), an open-source, Debian-based Linux OS that was perfect for the job. Despite the server's age, OMV lets me use it for file sharing, which is all I need. It doesn't bog the system down with a heavy OS.

It's easy to install on the server from a bootable USB drive created using Rufus. I installed the OS first, then found three 1TB drives lying around to use as storage. Once installed, I switched to managing the server through its web-based interface. I did a "quick format" of each drive as ext4 so they were readable and had room to store the files I was about to load on them.

The OMV web interface is straightforward and intuitive, making it easy to manage and monitor the health of the installed drives. Occasionally, the web UI fails to load. Or, I may have a network connectivity issue and need to connect my old monitor to the server to run ovm-firstaid from the prompt, but it's rare.
